title: IPv6 Router Advertisement Options for DNS Configuration
summary: Specifies IPv6 Router Advertisement options for advertising DNS recursive server addresses and a search list, and obsoletes RFC 6106 with a higher default lifetime for fewer expiries.

eli5.summary: Routers can announce which DNS helper to use, and the note lasts longer now.

questions: ipv6 router advertisement dns option type
subtitle: How an IPv6 router tells hosts which DNS servers and search domains to use, inside the Router Advertisement it already sends.

tldr.problem: Hosts that configure their IPv6 address by stateless autoconfiguration still need DNS server addresses and search suffixes, and manual setup or DHCPv6 may not be available.
tldr.mechanism: Two Router Advertisement options carry them: the RDNSS option (type 25) lists recursive DNS server addresses and the DNSSL option (type 31) lists search domains, each with a lifetime.
tldr.outcome: This document obsoletes RFC 6106 and raises the default lifetime so the options expire less often on links that lose packets.

today: RFC 8106 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 6106. No later RFC is listed as obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: Why Routers Announce DNS
sections.content:
IPv6 Neighbor Discovery and Stateless Address Autoconfiguration (SLAAC) give hosts addresses, default routers and a few other parameters, but not DNS information. Configuring laptops and other nomadic hosts by hand each time they join a network is infeasible, and DNS access is a fundamental requirement. DHCPv6 can supply it, but SLAAC cannot stand on its own in any practical network without some way to configure DNS.

The gap matters most in IPv6-only networks. In dual-stack networks it is less pressing as long as a DNS server is reachable over IPv4. This RFC defines two Router Advertisement (RA) options so that hosts can learn DNS settings from the same RA that configures the link.

RA-based configuration is useful where there is no DHCPv6 infrastructure or some hosts lack a DHCPv6 client. Where extra information must be distributed, DHCPv6 is likely used and RA-based DNS configuration may not be needed.
sections.eli5: When you join a new school, a sign at the door tells you where the office is. Here the router puts up a sign saying which helper to ask for addresses.

sections.title: Terms and Overview
sections.content:
A Recursive DNS Server (RDNSS) is a server that does recursive name resolution for the host. The RDNSS option carries its addresses. The DNS Search List (DNSSL) is the list of suffix domains a host tries when it looks up short, unqualified names, and the DNSSL option carries it.

The host keeps two data structures, together called the DNS Repository: the DNS Server List and the DNSSL. The Resolver Repository is what the host's resolver actually reads, such as /etc/resolv.conf or the Windows registry.

Routers must get their DNS information by manual configuration or some other mechanism such as DHCPv6. How routers do that automatically is out of scope.
sections.eli5: The router has a list of helpers. The host copies the list into its own notebook, which is what it checks whenever it needs an address.

sections.title: The RDNSS and DNSSL Options
sections.content:
Both options start with an 8-bit Type, an 8-bit Length in units of 8 octets, a 16-bit reserved field and a 32-bit Lifetime. The RDNSS option has Type 25 and then one or more 128-bit IPv6 addresses. Length is at least 3 for one address, and each extra address adds 2. All addresses in one option share a lifetime, so different lifetimes need separate options. Addresses may be link-local, in which case the resolver MUST use the matching link.

The DNSSL option has Type 31 and one or more domain names encoded as in Section 3.1 of RFC 1035, concatenated and not compressed. The field is padded with zeros to a multiple of 8 octets, and Length is at least 2.

For both, Lifetime is the maximum time in seconds the data MAY be used. It SHOULD by default be at least 3 * MaxRtrAdvInterval, the value 0xffffffff means infinity, and zero means the data MUST no longer be used.
sections.eli5: Each note says what kind it is, how long it is, how long it is good for, and then lists the helpers or the search words.

sections.title: How Hosts Process the Options
sections.content:
A host first checks validity. For RDNSS, Length must be at least 3 and satisfy (Length - 1) % 2 == 0, and the addresses should be unicast. For DNSSL, Length must be at least 2. Valid options SHOULD be copied in order into the DNS Repository and Resolver Repository; invalid ones MUST be discarded.

For each RDNSS address, a lifetime of zero deletes an existing entry, an entry already present just gets a new expiration time, and a new one is registered and placed first in the Resolver Repository. If the list is full, the entry that expires first is dropped. Addresses inside one option keep their order. DNSSL entries are handled the same way, and expired entries are removed. These entries have their own lifetimes, so they need not be dropped when the router lifetime expires.

Hosts conforming to this RFC MUST extract DNS information from RAs unless the user configured DNS statically. With several sources, hosts SHOULD keep information from all and are RECOMMENDED to store at least three addresses or domains in total. DHCP information SHOULD come first and take precedence. RAs using SEND MUST be preferred over those that do not, and over unauthenticated DHCP.
sections.eli5: The host checks the note is written properly, copies the helpers into its notebook, and crosses one out when it is told to or when its time runs out.

sections.title: Changes from RFC 6106
sections.content:
The main change is the lifetime. The old lower bound of 2 * MaxRtrAdvInterval was shown to let the options expire on links with a high rate of packet loss. The new default is 3 * MaxRtrAdvInterval, which matches the default router lifetime and lets entries survive three consecutive lost RAs containing DNS options.

Other changes: the text about sending a Router Solicitation before an RDNSS option expires is removed to avoid more multicast traffic; link-local RDNSS addresses are allowed; the limit of three addresses or domains is removed in favour of local policy; the kernel and user space synchronization guidance is removed; and SEND is described as a possible security mechanism rather than with SHOULD or RECOMMENDED.

Updated implementations still interoperate with those following RFC 6106.
sections.eli5: The sticky note used to peel off too soon when the mail was patchy, so now it is made to stick longer.

sections.title: Spoofed Advertisements
sections.content:
An attacker could send an RA with a fraudulent RDNSS address, steering hosts to an unintended DNS server, or a fraudulent DNSSL that makes an unqualified hostname resolve to an unintended host. The RFC says this is no worse than the existing ND attacks, since learning bad DNS data via RA cannot be worse than learning bad router information that way.

Secure Neighbor Discovery (SEND, RFC 3971) can sign all ND options, including these. Network devices should block rogue RAs carrying the options from unauthorized nodes, as switches already block rogue DHCPv6 servers. For a bogus search list, resolvers can follow the recommendations in RFC 1535, RFC 1536 and RFC 3646.
sections.eli5: A prankster could put up a fake sign pointing you to the wrong helper. Signed signs and guards at the door help stop that.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: In units of 8 octets; at least 3, plus 2 per extra address.

fields.name: Lifetime
fields.desc: Maximum seconds the addresses may be used; 0xffffffff means infinity, zero means stop using.
